subparts.author_conclusion: The two shaded geometric areas are equal for 0<a<b.
subparts.author_derivation: On the given y=1/x graph, substitute x=−u or use odd symmetry. The left signed integral ∫₋ᵦ⁻ᵃ1/x dx=ln(a/b) is the negative of the right signed integral ln(b/a). Their positive geometric areas therefore agree. Never identify a negative integral with a negative geometric area.
subparts.method: Author mathematical reasoning from the original task; explicit source support/absence recorded. This logical comparison is not an automated proof.

subparts.author_conclusion: The equality follows from y=1/x being odd, or the substitution u=−x with reversed bounds.
subparts.author_derivation: With 0<a<b, the substitution reverses limits b→a and introduces dx=−du, so the left signed integral is −ln(b/a). Negate it for the below-axis area. The book supplies the substitution proof on the next page; the answer-key remark supplies odd symmetry as an alternative.

subparts.author_conclusion: Zeros of the original denominator p₂(x) are excluded from the original quotient; cancellation does not restore the original function there.
subparts.author_derivation: A polynomial is continuous everywhere. A quotient of continuous polynomials is continuous wherever its denominator is nonzero. A common numerator factor may give a removable hole, but the original quotient is still undefined there. The source key says the denominator can take value zero.
subparts.method: Author mathematical reasoning from the original task; explicit source support/absence recorded. This logical comparison is not an automated proof.

subparts.author_conclusion: The polynomial x²−2x+3 is continuous for all real x.
subparts.author_derivation: It is a polynomial (equivalently a quotient with denominator 1), so it has no real denominator holes. The key additionally completes the square to (x−1)²+2≥2; positivity is true but is not needed to prove polynomial continuity.
